text: Γνωμικῶς δέ. Animi sententia, arbitrio. Non apte Picus. Quoad intellectum autem. Nam et βούλησις absolute, facultas est intellectum sequens; τὸ γνωμικὸν, ut ejus modum specialem opponit Maximus.
anchorLine: γνωμικῶς δὲ (c), πρὸς τὴν τοῦ κεκτημένου βούλησιν,
en: Gnomikōs de: 'animi sententia' means 'by choice' (arbitrio); Picus renders it unsuitably. As for the intellect: for boulēsis taken absolutely is also a faculty that follows the intellect; as for the gnomic (τὸ γνωμικόν), Maximus opposes its particular mode.

text: Πρὸς τὴν τοῦ ποιητοῦ τῶν ὅλων μυσταγωγίαν. Erat editis mend. μεταγωγίαν· quæ vox nihil apta, etsi reddere conatus est Picus, afflicta etiam illi significatione valde aliena, debere moveri desiderium nostrum ad placandum Deum. Exponit Maximus post utrumque Greg. aliosque Patres, peccati Adæ pravitatem, quod prius creaturis adjecerit animum, quam Deo illarum auctori; cum nec creaturis adjicere malum esset, si modo ordo servatus fuisset. Quæ Picus nihil intellexit. c. 33, quod erat δραστικήν, redditque Picus vim activam, emend. ex q. illa 43, ad Thal. διακριτικήν, quæ una vox ex Maximi instituto est.
anchorLine: γίαν (d) ἡμῶν κινεῖσθαι τὴν ἔφεσιν.
en: Pros tēn tou poiētou tōn holōn mystagōgian. The printed editions had, by mistake, metagōgian, a word quite unsuitable, though Picus tried to render it, and its meaning is far removed: that our desire ought to be moved to appease God. Maximus, after both Gregories and the other Fathers, expounds the depravity of Adam's sin: that he turned his mind first to creatures rather than to God their author, whereas it would not have been evil to turn to creatures if the order had been kept. Picus understood none of this. In ch. 33, where the text had drastikēn (and Picus rendered it 'active force'), emended from q. 43 of the Ad Thalassium to diakritikēn, a single word that is characteristic of Maximus's usage.

text: Στάσιν λαμβανούσης· Interquiescente, seu cessante; ne sensu medio ad spiritualia transeat; [continues on p-0631:] qua scilicet conspectis rebus libidine adhæret, nec ipsas in eis legere rationes, iisque ad spiritalia assurgere studet.
anchorLine: περὶ τὰς ἐπιφανείας τῶν ὁρατῶν, στάσιν λαμβανού-σης (e) διὰ τῆς μέσης αἰσθήσεως τῆς περὶ τὰ νοητά
en: Stasin lambanousēs: 'when it is at rest, or ceasing'; so that it may not pass through the middle sense to spiritual things; by which, once visible things are seen, it clings to them with desire, and does not read the principles in them nor strive through them to rise up to spiritual things.

text: Ἡ τοῦ νοῦ δύναμις. Sic emend. ex mss. cod. cum esset, Ἡ τοῦ νόμου δύναμις. Hæc enim mentis objecta sunt, non legis : corporum incorporeorumque ( seu spirituum ) notitia : non tamen ipsius Trinitatis, quoad quod quid est esse, cognitio. Unum hoc credit pia mens, ipsam esse οὐ τί ποτε κατ᾿ οὐσίαν ἐστὶν αὐθαδιζομένη · sibi ipsa per superbiam non arrogans, ut sciat quid illa sit per essentiam ; ὡς ὁ δαιμόνιος νοῦς · quasi hoc uni proprium dicat divinæ menti. Nihil boni Picus : Nullatenus secundum substantiam est contumax, velut infelix animus. De voce δαιμόνιος, multa Bud. et alii. Planus hic sensus, ut sit divina ac beata mens, ipse Deus, qui sic a se nihil arrogatam habet sui per essentiam notitiam : quod tamen, et sequentia ejus cap. desiderant tres Regii codd. quorum copia fuit. Si quis tamen ad diabolum trahere velit, qui sic αὐθαδίζεσθαι dicatur, ut est illius a peccato ἄνους ὁ λόγος, et alia quæ prosequitur Dionys. non pugno. Potest ille temeritate adyta velle perrumpere et inconcessa tentare : at non sana mens, ac quæ nititur fide.
anchorLine: μις (f) · τῆς δὲ τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος, κατὰ μόνην τὴν
en: Hē tou nou dynamis ('the power of the mind'). So emended from a manuscript codex; when it read 'the power of the law' (nomou). For these are objects of the mind, not of the law: knowledge of bodies and of incorporeal things (that is, spirits), but not of the Trinity itself as to knowledge of what it is. This one thing the pious mind believes, that it is 'in no way self-willed according to essence', not arrogating to itself through pride to know what it is by essence, as the 'demonic mind' does, as though he were saying that this belongs to the divine mind alone. Picus is no good here: his 'in no way is it contumacious according to substance, like an unhappy soul'. On the word daimonios, Budé and others say much. The sense here is plain: that the divine and blessed mind, God himself, who thus claims for himself no knowledge of himself by essence that he has not; but three royal codices, of which there was a supply, lack this and the following of the chapter. If anyone nevertheless wished to apply it to the devil, who is said thus to be self-willed, as his reason (logos) is senseless from sin, and the other things Dionysius pursues, I do not object. He may with rashness want to break into the inner sanctuaries and attempt what is forbidden; but not a sound mind, one that rests on faith.

text: Τὸ στηθύνιον τοῦ ἐπιθέματος. Vulg. uti reddidimus, Pectusculum elevationis. Syxt. interpr. impositionis, quod non ita videtur exprimere. Ibi Schol. Ταυτόν ἐστιν ἀφαίρεμα καὶ ἀφόρισμα καὶ ἐπίθεμα καὶ καρπώματα ἀπὸ τῶν θυσιῶν ἀφοριζόμενα Θεῷ, ἅπερ γίνεται μέρη τοῦ ἱερέως. Non male forsitan appositionis ; sive pectusculum appositum ac suppositum divinæ hostiæ, ac parti illi quæ peculiarius in Dei honorem cedebat, illique incendebatur. Eam mentem nostri Jac. de Janua Catholicon insinuavit. Eo forte Græcorum ritus collineat, cum massæ panis, ex qua Dominicum corpus conficiunt, complures micas offerentium nomine apponunt, sive supponunt, quas incertum an sacrificent. Non tamen in omnibus quadrat exemplum.
anchorLine: ματος (g)· τουτέστι, τῶν προσαγομένων τὴν χαρ-
en: To stēthynion tou epithematos ('the breast of the addition'). The Vulgate, as we have rendered it: 'breast of elevation'. The Sixtine translator has 'of imposition', which does not seem to express it. There the scholion reads: 'Epithema, aphairema, aphorisma and karpomata are the same: things set apart from the sacrifices for God, which become the priest's portions.' Perhaps not badly 'of apposition'; or the breast placed on and under the divine victim, and to that part which belonged more especially to God's honour, and was burnt there. Our Jacobus de Janua suggested this sense in the Catholicon. Perhaps the Greek rite aims at this, when from the loaf from which they make the Lord's body they add, or set under, several crumbs in the name of those offering, which it is uncertain whether they sacrifice. Yet the example does not fit in everything.

text: Τῶν ἐλεῖν βουλομένων. Sensus ipse planus. Securitatem hæc sonant, ejus, qui scientia ac virtute longe provectus sit, nec facile ex sensu ejusque libidine tentari aut lædi possit; qua sollicitudine moribus excultus, divinis animum intendit. Picus ἐλθεῖν habuit, ex quo nihil probati sensus elicere potuit.
anchorLine: ὡς ὑπὸ μηδενὸς τῶν ἐλεῖν βουλομένων (h) παντελῶς
en: Tōn elein boulomenōn ('of those wishing to catch'). The sense itself is plain. These words speak of the security of one far advanced in knowledge and virtue, who cannot easily be tempted or harmed by the sense and its lust; in such solicitude, cultivated in morals, he directs his mind to divine things. Picus had elthein ('to come'), from which he could draw no acceptable sense.

text: Λάκκους καλεῖ ἡ Γραφή. Lacus ac cisternas expressit Scriptura, intellexitque Maximus ; nec bene Picus puteis mutavit. Puteus namque ipse fons est, sed alta scaturigine ; λάκκοι, lacus et cisternæ, non sunt fontes, nec ullo latice manant, sed pluvialibus aquis replentur. Qua metaphora φερομένης ἄνωθεν τῆς ἐν πνεύματι γνώσεως, scientia spiritali e supernis, e cœlo veniente, has mystice cisternas, Maximus ait impleri. At nihil bene Picus. Plena sunt spiritali sursum tendente scientia. Sursum tendere et salire, id quidem fontium est, vivarumque in eis aquarum, at non Maximo intentum, vel ejus Græcis significatum. Cf. ad Thalass. q. 48.
anchorLine: νθʹ. Λάκκους καλεῖ ἡ Γραφὴ (i), τὰς δεκτικὰς τῶν
en: Lakkous kalei hē Graphē ('Scripture calls them lakkoi'). Scripture expressed 'lakes and cisterns', and Maximus understood it so; Picus did not do well to change it to 'wells'. For a well is itself a spring, with deep welling; but lakkoi, 'pits and cisterns', are not springs, nor do they flow from any stream, but are filled with rainwater. By this metaphor, knowledge in the Spirit being borne from above (spiritual knowledge from on high, coming from heaven), Maximus says these cisterns are mystically filled. But Picus is wrong throughout: 'they are full of spiritual knowledge tending upward.' To tend upward and leap is characteristic of springs and of the living waters in them, but not what Maximus intended, nor what his Greek signifies. Compare the Ad Thalassium, question 48.

text: Τὰς ἀοράτους συμπλοκὰς ὑπαλύσκειν. Ita nempe sæpe cautum victoriæ est, quod mora temporis ac fuga prœlii, res suas quis in tuto ponat ; sinatque hostem ipsum in se suas vires frangere : quo modo Fabius rem Romanam cunctando restituit. Quem sensum melius redderet, quod ex mss. emendandum putaveram, ὑπαναλίσκειν · quod sit, paulatim consumere sensimque deterere ; sed malui edita, ipsa non mala, relinquere. Male vero Picus, συμπλοκὰς ἀοράτους · invisibilia involucra.
anchorLine: ὑπαλύσκειν (k) ἐπιστάμενον νοῦν, μήτε φυσικὴν μετ-
en: Tas aoratous symplokas hypalyskein ('to slip away from the invisible entanglements'). For so, often, caution is the way to victory: by delay of time and avoidance of battle one puts one's goods in safety and lets the enemy himself break his strength upon one, as Fabius restored the Roman state by delaying. A sense better rendered by what I had thought should be emended from the manuscripts, hypanaliskein, which would mean 'to consume gradually and wear down'; but I preferred to leave the printed reading, itself not bad. Picus, however, did badly with 'symplokas aoratous': 'invisible wrappings'. (The editor reports the printed reading hypalyskein and offers a manuscript-based conjecture, hypanaliskein, which he did not adopt.)

text: Καὶ περιεκτικῆς ἐγκρατείας. Etiam cent. i, c. 2, ἡ περιεκτικὴ ἐγκράτεια · quo loco sugillati Obsop. et Gesner. dum prior acquisita ; alter, universalis reddit. Propius rem attigit Picus, dum coercente reddidit ; quæ scilicet contineat, teneatque ac coerceat animum, ne se adduci affectibus sinat : uti eo loco expositum a me fuit.
anchorLine: ἐκτικῆς ἐγκρατείας (l) καὶ ὑπομονῆς μύσας τὰς αἰ-
en: Kai periektikēs enkrateias ('and of the encompassing self-control'). Also in century 1, chapter 2: 'hē periektikē enkrateia'; at which place Obsopoeus and Gesner are criticised, since the first renders it 'acquired' and the other 'universal'. Picus came nearer the point, rendering it 'coercente' (restraining), that is, which contains and holds and restrains the mind so that it does not let itself be led by the passions, as was explained by me in that place.

text: Τὰ αἰσθητὰ πάντα. Luxatum textum secutus Picus, nihil apte reddidit : hoc est universa sensilia animæ. Sunt animæ et dicuntur, universi sensus, non sensilia. Illud ergo τουτέστι, τῆς ψυχῆς, allegoria est, τοῦ ἔξω τῆς πόλεως. quod ex codd. repræsento : sunt nempe sensilia, exteriora illa influentia in animam, per sensus, quasi incalus quosdam, a quibus diligenter cavendum, obstruendo eosdem sensus, cum per eos una cum sensilibus, hostis ingruit. Sunt hi fenestræ, per quas mors ascendit, Jerem. ix, quæ alia metaphora est, ejusdem sensus.
anchorLine: ψυχῆς· ἃς Ἑζεκίας ἐμφράττει· τὰ αἰσθητὰ πάντα (m)·
en: Ta aisthēta panta ('all the sensibles'). Picus followed a disordered text and rendered nothing aptly: 'that is, all the sense-objects of the soul'. They are of the soul, and 'all senses' is meant, not sense-objects. So the phrase 'that is, of the soul' is an allegory of 'outside the city'; which I restore from the codices: for the sense-objects are those outer influences upon the soul, through the senses, like certain entrances to be guarded against diligently by closing the senses themselves, since through them, together with the sensibles, the enemy enters. These are the windows through which death ascends, Jeremiah 9, another metaphor of the same sense. (The editor says he restores a reading from the codices.)

text: Διὰ τῆς ἀοριστίας. Significat hujus scientiæ, quam ἄληστον vocat, quasi animo indelebilem semperque in eo vigentem ; immensam quamdam vim, qua animus divinam infinitatem quadam velut proportione attingat, ejusque veritatis gloriam ac majestatem omni majorem infinito, quasi simulacro referat. Nam et τὸ ἀόριστον, Maximo aliisque theologis, inter divina nomina est, id ipsum quod Latinis immensitas. Hæc tam augusta, quis ex Pico audiat : Ex illa incertitudine superinfinitam effingit opinionem veritatis ? Quid hic incertitudo, ubi Deus altissimo modo attingitur ? Num quod δόξα, eaque incertitudinem exposcit ? At non hæc philosophica δόξα, opinio ; nutans scilicet animi assensus, cui falsum potest subesse, nec raro subest ; sed ipsa animorum circa Deum ἀεικινησία ; in beatis jam consummata ; hic in summis θεωρητικοῖς, quasi incepta.
anchorLine: εἰκονίζει διὰ τῆς ἀοριστίας (o) τὴν ὑπεράπει-
en: Dia tēs aoristias ('through indefiniteness'). It signifies this knowledge, which he calls 'unforgettable' (alēston), as if indelible in the mind and always flourishing in it; a certain immense power by which the mind, through a kind of proportion, reaches the divine infinity and represents, as in an image, the glory and majesty of that truth, greater than every infinite. For to aoriston too, in Maximus and other theologians, is among the divine names, that which Latins call 'immensity'. Who could hear, from Picus, such lofty matter rendered as 'from that uncertainty it fashions a superinfinite opinion of the truth'? What uncertainty is here, where God is reached in the highest manner? Does doxa demand uncertainty? But this is not the philosophical doxa, 'opinion', that is, a wavering assent of the mind to which falsehood can be present, and often is; rather it is the minds' own ceaseless motion toward God (aeikinēsia), already perfected in the blessed, here begun in the highest contemplatives.

text: Τῇ τοιαύτῃ τηκομένους φωνῇ. Clara allusio est ad I Esdr. iv, ubi describitur conatus hostium Judæorum, ut impedirent ædificationem templi ; quos Maximus tropologice dæmonas exponit, sic et ipsos et invidia contabescentes, quod spiritale in nobis Dei templum consurgere audiant, videantque, uti pluribus quæst. 56, ad Thal. Male itaque Picus διακονουμένους, dæmones habent hujusmodi voci inservientes. Non certe id muneris dæmonum ; etsi et ipsi simulate adjutores præferant exstruendi in nobis templi Domini, qui et hostes Judæorum, cum boni specie ac præstandæ virtutis, incautos spiritales in mali alicujus consensum trahunt, seu a recta virtutis via abducunt.
anchorLine: ἔχουσι τῇ τοιαύτῃ διατηκομένους φωνῇ (p), καὶ τοὺς
en: Tē toiautē tēkomenous phōnē ('wasting away at such a voice'). A clear allusion to 1 Esdras 4 [sic as printed], where the attempt of the Jews' enemies to hinder the building of the temple is described; Maximus explains these tropologically as the demons, who likewise waste away with envy when they hear and see the spiritual temple of God rising in us, as is shown at greater length in question 56 of the Ad Thalassium. So Picus is wrong in rendering diakonoumenous: 'demons who have such a voice serving it'. It is certainly not the demons' office, even if they too pretend to be helpers in building the Lord's temple in us, who, like the enemies of the Jews, with an appearance of good and of virtue to be shown, draw the unwary spiritual into consent to some evil or lead them away from the right path of virtue. (The editor reports a reading in the printed text, 'tēkomenous', which differs from the printed Greek 'diatētēkomenous'; and rejects Picus's rendering.)

text: Τοὺς ἐν αὐτῇ νόμους. Τρόπους hic etiam, ac sæpius alibi vocat Maximus, suntque res ipsæ consideratæ, ut ex eis aliquæ regulæ peti possunt ad informandos mores ; uti et λόγοι, res eædem sic quasi speculando in abstractione conceptæ, ac præcipue ut per eas animus assurgit, ut earum cognoscat auctorem, quem in illis velut expressum legit. Vide cent. 3, c. 6.
anchorLine: λόγους καὶ, τοὺς ἐν αὐτῇ νόμους (q) αὐτῷ
en: Tous en autē nomous ('the laws in it'). Here too, as often elsewhere, Maximus calls them tropoi ('modes'); and they are the things themselves considered, so that from them certain rules can be taken for forming morals; as also the logoi, the same things conceived, as it were, by contemplation in abstraction, and especially so that through them the mind rises to know their author, whom it reads as if expressed in them. See century 3, chapter 6.

text: Βοῶν ἀλαλήτως. Quasi non lingua, vel clamore ex ore exeunte ; sed qui in majori contentione virtutis ac scientiæ, uti ipse Maximus exponit, positus est. Sic Rom. viii : Στεναγμοῖς ἀλαλήτοις. Vulg. gemitibus inenarrabilibus ; possit et, animo tacitis. Hic nempe angelus est adjutor et salvans, quem Maximus μείζονα dicit σοφίας καὶ γνώσεως λόγον. Picus, Verbum sapientiæ et cognitione præstantius. Mihi simplicius, majorem (principem) sapientiæ ac scientiæ sermonem ; uti hic, sic et cap. 20 [continues] tione λόγου γνώσεως, qui nec prorsus μείζων, nisi comparatione ad reliquos sequentes. Non enim majus seu præstantius verbum, aut sermo vel ratio, sapientia ac scientia ; sed in illis major præstantia et intensio. Sermonem sapientiæ, ut dignissimum primo loco ponit Apostolus I Cor. viii, λόγον σοφίας ; hincque Maximus μείζονα dicere, maluerit, quam μείζονος λόγον σοφίας : tanquam principem sapientiæ sermonem, non majoris sapientiæ sermonem. Etiam, c. 41, supremam perfectionem in sapientia ponit : quæ sit ipsa finis, et se ad Deum immediate habeat.
anchorLine: βοῶν ἀλαλήτως (r)
en: Boōn alalētōs ('crying out unutterably'). As if not with the tongue, or with a shout from the mouth, but one set in a greater contention of virtue and knowledge, as Maximus himself explains. So in Romans 8: 'stenagmois alalētois', Vulgate 'with unspeakable groanings'; it could also be 'silent in spirit'. Here the angel is the helper and saviour, whom Maximus calls 'a greater word of wisdom and knowledge' (meizona sophias kai gnōseōs logon). Picus: 'a word of wisdom and surpassing knowledge'. To me, more simply, 'the greater (that is, the chief) word of wisdom and knowledge'; as here, so too in chapter 20, in the phrase 'logos of knowledge' which is not at all 'greater' except by comparison to the rest that follow. For 'greater' does not mean a larger or more excellent word, speech or reason, wisdom and knowledge; but in them there is greater excellence and intensity. The Apostle in 1 Cor. 8 [as printed] puts 'the word of wisdom' in first place as most worthy; and hence Maximus would prefer to say meizona rather than meizonos logon sophias, meaning the chief word of wisdom, not the word of a greater wisdom. Also in chapter 41 he places supreme perfection in wisdom, which is itself the end and has an immediate relation to God.

text: Παντὸς ἄρχειν πάθους τὸ προσφυὲς αἰσθητόν. Esse originem atque auctorem ; seu etiam per illud ejusque objectu, dæmonem, uti ipse Maximus, n fine cap.
anchorLine: αἰσθητόν (s). Ἄνευ γάρ τινος ὑποκειμένου, καὶ τὰς
en: Pantos archein pathous to prosphyes aisthēton ('the connatural sensible object rules every passion'). That is, to be the origin and author; or also, through it and its object, the demon, as Maximus himself says at the end of the chapter. (Last two characters before 'fine cap.' are an inked blob.)

text: Ἐν τῇ συνοχῇ τῆς τοῦ καθ᾿ ἕκαστον εἴδους μονιμότητος. In continua cujusque speciei perennitate, seu conservatione : qua scilicet individua alia aliis continua serie succedunt ac cohærent ; quippe alia ex aliis deducta ; quæ propria τοῦ συνεχοῦς acceptio est, ut est talis contactus ; de quo Suid. in voce συνοχή. Non bene Picus, Sermones percipiuntur ex solida cujuscunque speciei cohærentia.
anchorLine: τοῦ καθ᾿ ἕκαστον εἴδους γνωρίζονται μονιμότητος (t)·
en: En tē synochē tēs tou kath' hekaston eidous monimotētos. 'In the continuous perpetuity, or conservation, of each species': in which individuals succeed and cohere with one another in an unbroken series, being derived one from another; which is the proper sense of 'the continuous', as of such a contact; on which see Suidas under the word synochē. Picus is not good here: 'Words are perceived from the solid coherence of any species whatever.' [The marker letter is a squashed italic glyph that could be l or t in both the text and the note; read as t.]

text: Τελείως τὸ κατὰ τῶν πνευμάτων τῆς πονηρίας ἀνεδήσατο κράτος. Victoriam, palmam retulit. Sic Greg. in Basilio, de Maximino Christianos persequente τὸ τῆς ἀσεβείας κράτος ἀναδήσασθαι. Palmam et coronam impietatis mereri. Bud. At, Picus, Plane se gesserit impudenter, etc., quæ mera inscitia est : ut quod statim sequitur de Juda et Jerusalem, quibus eamdem derelictionis iram accidere ait Maximus, quæ Ezechiæ, dum reddit, sed Judas et Jerusalem ingruunt. Dicas loqui de hostibus ipsius Ezechiæ. Sic nullo sensu omnia.
anchorLine: κράτος (u), καὶ μὴ τὴν δέουσαν εὐχαριστίαν ἀνά-
en: Teleiōs to kata tōn pneumatōn tēs ponērias anedēsato kratos. 'He won victory, the palm.' So Gregory in the Basil [oration], speaking of Maximinus persecuting Christians: 'to bind on the power (kratos) of impiety'; 'to deserve the palm and crown of impiety', Budé. But Picus has 'he would have behaved quite shamelessly', etc., which is sheer ignorance: as in what immediately follows about Judah and Jerusalem, on whom Maximus says the same wrath of abandonment falls, which in Picus' rendering of Hezekiah's case ('but Judah and Jerusalem rush in') [the editor says] you would think he was speaking of Hezekiah's own enemies. Thus everything is nonsense.

text: Τοὺς ἐπὶ κρείττοσι φανέντας ἀγνώμονας. Τὸ κρεῖττον, haud raro pro virtute sumitur ; nec hic aliter Maximus. De illa enim Providentia sermo est, qua vitiis et affectibus laborare sinimur, ut ad modestiam gratique animi sensum in virtutibus componamur, summeque Deo exosam illique contrariam superbiam, longe excutiamus. Sic non bene Picus, rebus prosperis, rebus secundis ; aut certe minus explicate.
anchorLine: χρείττοσι φανέντας ἀγνώμονας (v), καὶ τὴν πεῖραν
en: Tous epi kreittosi phanentas agnōmonas ('those who appear ungrateful for better things'). To kreitton ('the better') is often taken for 'virtue', and Maximus here no differently. For the discussion is of that Providence by which we are allowed to labour under vices and passions, so that we may be set in order toward modesty and a grateful mind in the virtues, and may cast far from us pride, which is most hateful to God and opposed to him. Thus Picus is not good with 'in prosperous circumstances, in favourable circumstances'; or at any rate it is less well explained.

anchorLine: et nubibus mandabo ne pluant super eam ⁸¹.

text: Ὑφ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ ζημιούμενος. Ipse sibi auctor amittendi salutis finem (Deum scilicet) ejusque jacturæ. Quod sic clarum, Picus, hoc, et seq. cap., a seipso afficiens injuria, contumelia ; quod nimis crassum ac supinum est.
anchorLine: ἑαυτοῦ, φημὶ δὲ τὸν Θεὸν, ζημιούμενος (x). Ὁ δὲ
en: Hyph' heautou zēmioumenos ('being penalised by himself'). He is himself the author of losing the end of salvation (that is, God) and of its loss. What is thus clear, Picus (here and in the following chapter) [renders as] 'afflicting himself with injury, insult'; which is far too crude and careless.

text: Τὴν πρὸς πάντα τὰ ὄντα γνωμικὴν ἀπογένεσιν. Uti γένεσις natura est ; et γίνεσθαι, oriri, in rerum naturam produci ; sic ἀπογένεσις, desitio atque nihilum. Mens ergo laudabiliter moritur, cum sic se habet ad res alias, ac si ne esset quidem ; quod illis superatis, uni Deo et auctori tota impenditur. Non satis Picus, spontaneam omnium quæ sunt privationem ; quæ esset paupertatis definitio, non excellentiæ ejus status, quem Maximus intendit describere. Hesych. ἀπογενόμενοι, ἀποθανόντες.
anchorLine: πρὸς πάντα τὰ ὄντα γνωμικὴν ἀπογένεσιν (y), μεθ᾿
en: Tēn pros panta ta onta gnōmikēn apogenesin ('the gnomic departure-from-being with respect to all things'). As genesis is 'nature', and gignesthai is 'to arise, to be brought forth into the nature of things', so apogenesis is 'cessation and nothingness'. The mind thus dies laudably when it stands so toward other things as if they were not even there; which things being surpassed, the whole is spent on God alone and its author. Picus is not satisfactory with 'a spontaneous privation of all things that are'; that would be a definition of poverty, not of the excellence of the state which Maximus means to describe. Hesychius: 'apogenomenoi' = 'apothanontes' (those who have died).

text: Ἐν ᾗ τὸ καθ᾿ ὁμοίωσιν ἀναφαίνεσθαι πέφυκε κάλλος. In quo complemento divinæ operationis, elucet similitudinis decor : id quod est ad similitudinem. Itaque ponit Maximus similitudinis rationem in imitatione divinæ bonitatis, quæ sit in nobis virtutum cultu et actione : imaginis vero rationem, in perfectissima illa omnium circa Deum uniformi scientia, quæ expressio sit divinæ veritatis. Non bene Picus : In quæ pro similitudine relucere solet quoddam ornamentum : quasi τὸ, ἐν ᾗ, referat τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς, non τὸ, συμπλήρωσις τῆς θείας ἐνεργείας. Utrumque sane et similitudo et imago, in anima elucet, non pro ejus substantia (quod attinet ad Maximi hic scopum) sed prout vel virtute vel scientia pollet, Deique in se bonitatem ac veritatem utraque refert.
anchorLine: πέφυκε κάλλος (z) ·
en: En hē to kath' homoiōsin anaphainesthai pephyke kallos ('in which the beauty according to likeness is by nature made to appear'). In this completion of the divine operation the beauty of likeness shines forth, which is to say what belongs to likeness. Maximus thus places the principle of likeness in the imitation of divine goodness, which is in us through the cultivation and practice of the virtues; and the principle of image in that most perfect, uniform knowledge of all things concerning God, which is the expression of divine truth. Picus is wrong: 'in the things for which a certain ornament is wont to shine as likeness', as if 'in which' (en hē) referred to what belongs to the soul, and not to 'the completion of the divine operation'. Both likeness and image shine in the soul, not according to its substance (which is not Maximus's concern here) but as it is strong in virtue or knowledge, and each represents God's goodness and truth in it.

text: Ἁπάντων τὴν ψυχὴν ἐξαρπάζουσα. Quod ait Maximus, extrahere charitatem ab omnibus creatis animam, Deoque quasi commiscere ac illi adjungere, fœdo Picus errore : Omnium rapit animam, tum eorum quæ generationi et corruptioni sunt obnoxia, etc. Ergo etiam pecorum et stirpium, hæcque ipsa charitatis capacia sunt, et ut sic Deo copulentur ?
anchorLine: ἀπάντων τὴν ψυχὴν ἐξαρπάζουσα (a)
en: Hapantōn tēn psychēn exarpazousa ('snatching the soul from all things'). What Maximus says, that charity draws the soul out from all created things, and as it were mingles it with God and joins it to him, Picus renders with foul error: 'it seizes the soul of all, including those things which are subject to generation and corruption', etc. So then of cattle and plants too, and are these themselves capable of charity, and so joined to God?

text: Πνεῦμα ἐπιστήμης. Habent LXX, πνεῦμα εὐσεβείας. Vulg. Spiritus pietatis. Ipse Maximus, cent. iv, ex his quinque c. 79 et 80, πνεῦμα εὐσεβείας et ipse habet. Arab. veræ religionis. Verum hæc ex Hebr. non prodierunt immediate. Hebr. unum idemque nomen est, quod statim seq. timor redditur. Ac forte scripserint οἱ LXX πνεῦμα εὐλαβείας : qui sit spiritus timoris casti, modesti, reverentialis ac religiosi. Videtur hic Maximus ἐπιστήμην pro prudentia usurpare, ac particulari judicio agibilium ; ut et γνῶσιν, pro judicio universali, ac quo rerum rationes comprehendamus. Alioqui notum quid ἐπιστήμη, et scientia stricte dictæ, philosophis.
anchorLine: πνεῦμα γνώσεως, πνεῦμα ἐπιστήμης (b), πνεῦμα
en: Pneuma epistēmēs ('spirit of knowledge'). The Septuagint has 'spirit of piety' (eusebeias); the Vulgate 'spirit of piety'. Maximus himself, in century 4, in these five at chapters 79 and 80, also has 'spirit of piety'. The Arabic: 'of true religion'. But these did not come immediately from the Hebrew. In the Hebrew it is one and the same word, which is immediately afterward rendered 'fear'. And perhaps the Seventy wrote 'spirit of reverence' (eulabeias): which is the spirit of chaste, modest, reverential and religious fear. Maximus here seems to use epistēmē for prudence, and for particular judgement of matters to be done; as also gnōsis for universal judgement, by which we comprehend the principles of things. Otherwise it is well known what epistēmē is, and what knowledge in the strict sense is, for philosophers. (The editor offers a conjecture on the Septuagint reading: eulabeias for eusebeias.)
